what_it_does: Modern solid-state drives can be organized in RAID arrays (where data is spread and duplicated across several drives so that any single failed drive can be reconstructed). When a write does not fill a complete data stripe, the drive must temporarily record a partial parity — essentially a partial checksum needed to maintain data integrity — and this bookkeeping creates extra write traffic that slows things down and wears out the drives faster. ZRAID exploits a little-known built-in buffer called the Zone Random Write Area (ZRWA) — a small scratch region inside each drive that accepts out-of-order writes — to stage and accumulate these partial checksums in place before the full stripe is committed, rather than logging them to a separate reserved zone. By using this existing hardware buffer as a temporary holding area, ZRAID avoids the extra write round-trips that previously caused the bottleneck, reducing wasted write traffic and extending drive lifespan.
